# 2 Kings Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 233v–234v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_013_page_001.jpg, 2KI_013_page_002.jpg, 2KI_013_page_003.jpg

---

**1** In the twenty-third year of King Joash of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king of Israel in Samaria. He reigned for seventeen years.

**2** He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, following the same sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into. He never abandoned them.

**3** So the LORD's anger burned against Israel, and he handed them over to King Hazael of Aram and his son Ben-hadad — again and again.

**4** But Jehoahaz pleaded with the LORD, and the LORD listened, because he could see how severely the king of Aram was crushing Israel.

**5** The LORD provided a deliverer for Israel, and they escaped from Aramean domination. The Israelites returned to living in their own homes as they had before.

**6** Even so, they did not abandon the sins that the house of Jeroboam had embedded in Israel. They kept right on in them. The Asherah pole still stood in Samaria.

**7** Jehoahaz's army had been reduced to almost nothing: fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand infantry. The king of Aram had crushed them — ground them to dust like grain on a threshing floor.

**8** Everything else about Jehoahaz's reign — all he did and his accomplishments — is recorded in the court history of the kings of Israel.

**9** Jehoahaz died and was buried in Samaria. His son Joash succeeded him.

**10** In the thirty-seventh year of King Joash of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king of Israel in Samaria. He reigned sixteen years.

**11** He too did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He never turned away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat; he continued in all of them.

**12** Everything else about Joash — all he did, including his war against King Amaziah of Judah — is recorded in the court history of the kings of Israel.

**13** Joash died, and Jeroboam succeeded him on the throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.

**14** Elisha was now dying. King Joash of Israel went to visit him. He wept over the prophet, crying out, "My father! My father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!" — the same words Elisha himself had cried when Elijah was taken.

**15** Elisha said, "Get a bow and some arrows." The king brought them.

**16** "Take the bow in your hands," Elisha told him. The king gripped the bow, and Elisha placed his own hands over the king's hands.

**17** "Open the east window," Elisha said. He opened it. "Now shoot!" The king shot. Elisha declared, "The LORD's arrow of victory! Victory over Aram! You will completely defeat the Arameans at Aphek."

**18** Then Elisha said, "Now take the arrows and strike the ground." The king struck the ground three times and stopped.

**19** The man of God was furious with him. "You should have struck the ground five or six times!" he said. "Then you would have completely destroyed Aram. Now you will defeat them only three times."

**20** Elisha died and was buried. Every spring, Moabite raiding parties would cross into Israelite territory.

**21** One day, some Israelites were burying a man when they spotted a raiding party approaching. In a panic, they threw the body into Elisha's tomb. The moment the corpse touched Elisha's bones, the man came back to life and stood up on his feet.

**22** King Hazael of Aram had oppressed Israel throughout Jehoahaz's entire reign.

**23** But the LORD was gracious to Israel and showed them compassion. He turned his attention back to them — because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He was not willing to destroy them, and he has not banished them from his presence to this day.

**24** When Hazael died, his son Ben-hadad became king in his place.

**25** Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz recaptured from Ben-hadad the cities that Hazael had taken from his father in battle. Joash defeated him three times and recovered the Israelite towns.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 4 — God hears despite unfaithfulness:** This is one of the most theologically generous moments in Kings. Jehoahaz pleads, and God listens — not because of repentance (v.6 makes clear they didn't repent), but because God saw their suffering. Compassion, not merit, drives the response.

**Verse 7 — "ground them to dust":** The military statistics are devastating: fifty cavalry, ten chariots, ten thousand infantry. This is a broken state, not a functioning army. The threshing-floor metaphor is visceral — Aram has literally processed Israel like grain.

**Verse 14 — Elisha's deathbed:** The king's cry echoes 2:12 — the same words Elisha spoke when Elijah ascended. The prophet who inherited the mantle now dies like any mortal. But the echo creates continuity: prophetic power transmits through generations, even through death (as v.21 will prove).

**Verse 19 — Elisha's fury:** The prophet is angry because the king's half-hearted obedience limits what God can do. Three strikes, three victories. Five or six would have been total annihilation of the Aramean threat. The lesson: the scope of divine action is tied to the depth of human commitment.

**Verse 21 — The miracle at the tomb:** Even dead, Elisha's bones carry resurrection power. This story functions as the final exclamation point on the Elisha cycle. His ministry began with inheriting double the spirit of Elijah; it ends with power that outlasts his own death.

**Verse 23 — The patriarchal covenant:** This is the only time in all of Kings that God's covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is explicitly cited. Israel has no merit to claim. They have only the ancient promise — and it holds.

*— PNEUMA*
